message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"2.41","text":"And when I, Clement, heard this, I said, “Truly I rejoice and acknowledge my gratitude to God, the benefactor in every respect. Yet he himself knows that I shall not be able to think anything except to think about everything in God’s favor. Therefore, do not suppose that I am asking because I doubt what has been said by God or even what will yet be said, but so that, once I myself have learned, I may also be able to teach another who wishes to learn in a fair-minded way. So tell me what false things have been added to the Scriptures and how they prove to be actually false.”\n\nPeter answered, “Even if you had not asked me, as I proceeded through the arguments in their proper order, I would have supplied the demonstration I promised. Nevertheless, hear how the Scriptures tell many falsehoods about him, as you will discover when you read them.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"κατὰ πάντα εὐεργέτῃ θεῷ","chosen":"God, the benefactor in every respect","rationale":"κατὰ πάντα presents God as beneficent in every respect, not merely as the benefactor of all objects."},{"source_quote":"τὰ πάντα ὑπὲρ θεοῦ φρονεῖν","chosen":"to think about everything in God’s favor","rationale":"ὑπὲρ θεοῦ indicates thought favorable to or in defense of God; an alternative is “to hold every opinion in defense of God.”"},{"source_quote":"εὐγνωμόνως μαθεῖν θέλοντα","chosen":"who wishes to learn in a fair-minded way","rationale":"εὐγνωμόνως can describe a reasonable, well-disposed, or appreciative manner; “fair-minded” suits the disposition of the prospective learner."},{"source_quote":"τὰ προσκείμενα ψευδῆ ταῖς γραφαῖς","chosen":"what false things have been added to the Scriptures","rationale":"προσκείμενα describes material placed alongside or added to the writings; the context treats γραφαί as authoritative Scriptures."},{"source_quote":"πῶς ὅτι ὄντως ψευδῆ τυγχάνει","chosen":"how they prove to be actually false","rationale":"The combination πῶς ὅτι is unusual but intelligibly asks how the alleged additions turn out in fact to be false."},{"source_quote":"αὐτοῦ πολλὰ καταψεύδονται αἱ γραφαί","chosen":"the Scriptures tell many falsehoods about him","rationale":"καταψεύδομαι with the genitive means to speak falsely against someone; “him” refers contextually to God."},{"source_quote":"ἐντυγχάνων αὐταῖς","chosen":"when you read them","rationale":"ἐντυγχάνω with writings commonly means to encounter them by reading; the more literal alternative is “when you engage with them.”"}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"2.42","text":"The things about to be said will suffice by way of example. I do not think, my friend Clement, that anyone who retains even a little affection and gratitude toward God will be able to accept, or so much as hear, the things said against him. But how is it possible for anyone to have a soul committed to sole rule and to become devout after having assumed beforehand that there are many gods and not one? And even if there is one, who, finding him implicated in many absurdities, will strive to become devout, in the hope that the origin of all things, because of the absurdities inherent in his own nature, will not pursue the wrongdoings of others?","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"οὐκ οἶμαι δέ ... εἰ δυνήσεταί τις","chosen":"I do not think ... that anyone ... will be able","rationale":"Although εἰ formally can introduce “whether,” after the negative οἶμαι the contextual force is an emphatic doubt that anyone could do so."},{"source_quote":"στοργὴν καὶ εὐγνωμοσύνην","chosen":"affection and gratitude","rationale":"στοργή denotes affectionate attachment, while εὐγνωμοσύνη here naturally denotes grateful appreciation toward God."},{"source_quote":"μοναρχικὴν ψυχὴν","chosen":"a soul committed to sole rule","rationale":"The literal “monarchical soul” means a disposition affirming one sovereign God; “monotheistic soul” is possible but would replace the author’s monarchy imagery."},{"source_quote":"προειληφότα","chosen":"having assumed beforehand","rationale":"The participle denotes adopting a prior conception or assumption."},{"source_quote":"εἰ δὲ καὶ εἷς","chosen":"even if there is one","rationale":"“God” is elliptically understood from the preceding contrast between many gods and one."},{"source_quote":"τὴν τῶν ὅλων ἀρχὴν","chosen":"the origin of all things","rationale":"ἀρχή may mean origin, first principle, or ruler; “origin” fits the description of God as the source of everything, while “ruler of all” remains possible."},{"source_quote":"μὴ ἐπέρχεσθαι τὰ ἄλλων ἀδικήματα","chosen":"will not pursue the wrongdoings of others","rationale":"ἐπέρχομαι can mean to come against, visit, or punish; “pursue” preserves the judicial implication without making punishment explicit."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"2.43","text":"Therefore, far be it from us to believe either that the Master of all, “who created heaven and earth” and everything in them, shares sovereignty with others, or that he lies—for if he lies, who then tells the truth?—or that he “tests” as though ignorant—and who then has foreknowledge? If he “deliberates” and “changes his mind,” who then is perfect in understanding and steadfast in purpose? If he “is jealous,” who then is beyond comparison? If he “hardens hearts,” who then makes wise? If blind and deaf, who then has granted sight and hearing? If he advises defrauding, who then practices justice? If he “mocks,” who then is sincere? If he is powerless, who then can do all things? If he acts unjustly, who then is just? If he “creates evils,” who then will do good things? If he does evil things, who then does good things?","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἀπείη πιστεύειν","chosen":"far be it from us to believe","rationale":"The impersonal optative expresses emphatic rejection; “from us” is supplied by the conventional English construction without identifying a narrower subject."},{"source_quote":"ἑτέροις συνάρχει","chosen":"shares sovereignty with others","rationale":"συνάρχω means to rule jointly with others, not merely to coexist with them."},{"source_quote":"πειράζει ὡς ἀγνοῶν","chosen":"“tests” as though ignorant","rationale":"πειράζω may mean test or tempt; the following ὡς ἀγνοῶν makes the acquisition of unknown information through testing the relevant idea."},{"source_quote":"ἐνθυμεῖται","chosen":"“deliberates”","rationale":"The verb can mean considers, reflects, or deliberates; “deliberates” highlights the alleged lack of already perfected understanding."},{"source_quote":"μεταμελεῖται","chosen":"“changes his mind”","rationale":"The verb may mean regrets or changes one’s mind; the contrast with being steadfast in purpose favors the latter here."},{"source_quote":"εἰ δὲ τυφλοὶ καὶ κωφοί","chosen":"If blind and deaf","rationale":"The Greek has plural adjectives but no expressed subject or verb. The compact English preserves that ellipsis; context may imply “if people are made blind and deaf,” but causation is not explicit in the supplied wording."},{"source_quote":"δικαιοσύνην νομιτεύει","chosen":"practices justice","rationale":"νομιτεύω can mean to observe something as customary or lawful; here it contrasts just conduct with advising fraud. “Regards justice as law” is also possible."},{"source_quote":"ἐνπαίζει","chosen":"“mocks”","rationale":"The verb denotes mocking or making sport of someone; “deceives” is possible in some contexts but is not required here."},{"source_quote":"κακὰ κτίζει","chosen":"“creates evils”","rationale":"The rendering preserves both the creation verb and the plural substantive κακά rather than generalizing the claim as merely “causes evil.”"}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ἐνπαίζει","issue":"The supplied print uses the unassimilated spelling ἐνπαίζει where the normalized spelling is commonly ἐμπαίζει. The form remains intelligible and does not require alteration.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"καὶ ’ τίς ἀγαθὰ πράξει;","issue":"An isolated high mark appears between καὶ and τίς. It has no evident syntactic function and is most plausibly editorial or typographical punctuation.","proposed_reading":"καὶ τίς ἀγαθὰ πράξει;","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"2.44","text":"If he desires “the fat mountain,” to whom do all things belong? If he lies, who then tells the truth? If he dwells in a tent, who then is uncontainable? If he longs for fat-smoke and sacrifices and sacrificial victims and libations, who then needs nothing, and who is holy, and who is pure, and who is perfect? If he delights in lamps and lampstands, who then set the luminaries in heaven? If he dwells with thick gloom and darkness and tempest and smoke, who then, being light, illuminates the greatest age? If he approaches with trumpets and loud cries and missiles and arrows, who then is the calm awaited by all? If he himself loves wars, who then desires peace? If he himself “creates” “the evils,” who then fashions good things? If he himself is without affection, who then loves humanity? If he himself is not faithful concerning what he promises, who then will be trusted? If he himself loves wicked people and adulterers and murderers, who then will be a just judge? If he himself changes his mind, who then is steadfast? If he himself chooses evil people, who then welcomes good people?","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὸ πῖον ὄρος","chosen":"“the fat mountain”","rationale":"πῖον literally describes something fat or rich and may imply a fertile or luxuriant mountain; the concrete “fat” image is retained because the phrase is quoted."},{"source_quote":"ἀχώρητος","chosen":"uncontainable","rationale":"The adjective denotes one who cannot be contained, confined, or accommodated within a place."},{"source_quote":"κνίσης","chosen":"fat-smoke","rationale":"κνίση denotes the greasy smoke or savor rising from burning fat; the compact rendering preserves both the material and sacrificial imagery."},{"source_quote":"κνίσης καὶ θυσιῶν καὶ θυμάτων καὶ προσχύσεων","chosen":"fat-smoke and sacrifices and sacrificial victims and libations","rationale":"The repeated conjunctions and the distinction between sacrifices, victims, and poured offerings are retained."},{"source_quote":"ἐν γνόφῳ καὶ σκότῳ καὶ θυέλλῃ καὶ καπνῷ σύνεστιν","chosen":"dwells with thick gloom and darkness and tempest and smoke","rationale":"σύνεστιν literally means “is together with”; “dwells with” conveys association while preserving all four atmospheric images."},{"source_quote":"τὸν μέγιστον αἰῶνα","chosen":"the greatest age","rationale":"αἰών may denote an age, eternity, or a world-order. “Age” is the most direct rendering, while “the greatest world” remains a possible contextual interpretation."},{"source_quote":"βολίδων καὶ τοξευμάτων","chosen":"missiles and arrows","rationale":"βολίδες are thrown projectiles or bolts, while τοξεύματα are things shot from a bow; the two images are kept distinct."},{"source_quote":"ἡ τῶν ὅλων προσδόκιμος γαλήνη","chosen":"the calm awaited by all","rationale":"προσδόκιμος means expected or awaited, and τῶν ὅλων can refer to everyone or to all things collectively."},{"source_quote":"ἄστοργος","chosen":"without affection","rationale":"The adjective denotes absence of natural or familial affection; “unloving” is a broader alternative."},{"source_quote":"μεταμελεῖται","chosen":"changes his mind","rationale":"Here the verb is contrasted with βέβαιος, one who is stable or steadfast; “regrets” is also lexically possible."},{"source_quote":"προσίεται","chosen":"welcomes","rationale":"The verb can mean admits, receives, or accepts; “welcomes” provides a natural contrast with choosing evil people."}],"source_issues":[]}]}
